# C++ Debugging (GDB + Valgrind + Sanitizers)

## Overview

| Tool | When |
|---|---|
| **GDB** | Step through code, inspect variables, set breakpoints, post-mortem on core dumps |
| **Valgrind (Memcheck)** | Detect memory leaks, use-after-free, invalid reads/writes |
| **Valgrind (Callgrind)** | Profile: call graphs, instruction counts, cache misses |
| **AddressSanitizer (ASan)** | Fast memory error detection — much faster than Valgrind |
| **UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan)** | Detect UB: integer overflow, null deref, shift errors |
| **GDB + core dump** | Post-mortem analysis of crashed programs |

**Start with ASan.** It's the cheapest runtime checker. Move to GDB when you need step-through. Valgrind when you need heap profiling or ASan can't be compiled in.

## Prerequisites

```bash
# Install tools
apt-get install -y gdb valgrind

# Ensure core dumps are enabled
ulimit -c unlimited
echo "/tmp/core.%e.%p" | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
```

## Recipe 1: Compile with Debug Symbols

Always compile with `-g -O0` for debugging:

```bash
g++ -g -O0 -Wall -Wextra -o myprog myprog.cpp
```

For sanitizers:
```bash
g++ -g -O0 -fsanitize=address -o myprog_asan myprog.cpp
g++ -g -O0 -fsanitize=undefined -o myprog_ubsan myprog.cpp
g++ -g -O0 -fsanitize=address,undefined -o myprog_full myprog.cpp
```

CMake:
```bash
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address" ..
```

## Recipe 2: GDB Quick Start

```bash
# Launch program under GDB
gdb --args ./myprog arg1 arg2

# Attach to running process
gdb -p <pid>

# Post-mortem on core dump
gdb ./myprog /tmp/core.myprog.12345
```

### Essential GDB Commands

| Command | Alias | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `help cmd` | `h cmd` | Help |
| `run` | `r` | Start program |
| `break file:line` | `b file:42` | Set breakpoint |
| `break func` | `b parseInput` | Break on function |
| `break file:line if x>5` | | Conditional breakpoint |
| `tbreak file:line` | `tb` | One-shot breakpoint |
| `next` | `n` | Next line (step over) |
| `step` | `s` | Step into function |
| `finish` | `fin` | Run until current function returns |
| `continue` | `c` | Continue execution |
| `until N` | `u` | Run until line N (same function) |
| `print expr` | `p x` | Print expression |
| `display expr` | `disp x` | Auto-print on every stop |
| `print/x var` | | Print in hex |
| `print *ptr@10` | | Print 10 elements at pointer |
| `explore var` | | Interactive exploration of variable |
| `backtrace` | `bt` | Full call stack |
| `backtrace full` | `bt full` | Stack + all locals |
| `frame N` | `f` | Switch to stack frame N |
| `up` / `down` | | Move up/down call stack |
| `info locals` | `i lo` | Show all local variables |
| `info args` | `i ar` | Show function arguments |
| `info registers` | `i r` | Show CPU registers |
| `info break` | `i b` | List breakpoints |
| `delete N` | `d` | Delete breakpoint N |
| `disable N` | `dis` | Disable breakpoint N |
| `enable N` | `en` | Enable breakpoint N |
| `layout src` | | TUI source view (`ctrl-x a` to toggle) |
| `list` | `l` | Show source around current line |
| `watch var` | | Break when variable changes |
| `set var = value` | | Modify variable at runtime |
| `call func(args)` | | Call a function from debugger |
| `quit` | `q` | Exit GDB |

## Recipe 3: Inspecting Pointers and Data Structures

```gdb
# Print at a pointer (dereference)
(gdb) p *ptr

# Print array at pointer (printing 20 elements)
(gdb) p *(ptr@20)

# Print STL container (GDB pretty-printers needed, usually auto-loaded)
(gdb) p vec
# $1 = std::vector of length 5, capacity 8 = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

# If pretty-printers not loaded:
sudo apt-get install libstdc++6-13-dbg  # or your GCC version

# Print map contents
(gdb) p mymap
# $2 = std::map with 3 elements = {["a"] = 1, ["b"] = 2, ["c"] = 3}

# Print string
(gdb) p str.c_str()
# $3 = 0x555555... "hello world"
```

## Recipe 4: Valgrind Memory Analysis

```bash
# Basic memory error check (the most common use case)
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./myprog arg1

# Track origins of uninitialized values
valgrind --track-origins=yes ./myprog

# Suppress known issues with suppressions file
valgrind --suppressions=valgrind.sup --leak-check=full ./myprog

# Generate suppressions interactively (Valgrind will prompt you)
valgrind --gen-suppressions=all --leak-check=full ./myprog
```

### What Valgrind Detects

| Error | What it means |
|---|---|
| `Invalid read/write` | Accessing memory you shouldn't (out-of-bounds, freed, etc.) |
| `Use of uninitialised value` | Reading from uninitialized memory |
| `Conditional jump depends on uninitialised value` | Branching on garbage |
| `Invalid free` | Double-free, freeing non-malloc'd memory |
| `Mismatched free/delete` | `free()` on `new`, `delete` on `malloc()` |
| `N bytes in M blocks are definitely lost` | Memory leak — no pointers to the memory anywhere |
| `N bytes in M blocks are indirectly lost` | Leaked via another leaked block |
| `N bytes in M blocks are possibly lost` | Interior pointer — might still be reachable |
| `N bytes in M blocks are still reachable` | Not freed but program still holds a pointer |

## Recipe 5: Valgrind Profiling (Callgrind)

```bash
# Generate callgrind data
valgrind --tool=callgrind ./myprog

# View with KCachegrind GUI (if available)
kcachegrind callgrind.out.<pid>

# Or view text summary
callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.<pid>
```

## Recipe 6: AddressSanitizer (Fast Runtime Checking)

```bash
# Compile with ASan
g++ -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o myprog myprog.cpp

# Run — ASan reports immediately on any violation
./myprog

# ASan output looks like:
# =================================================================
# ==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x...
# READ of size 4 at 0x... thread T0
#     #0 0x... in main myprog.cpp:42
# ...stack trace...
# =================================================================
```

## Recipe 7: GDB with Core Dumps (Post-Mortem)

When a program crashes (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, etc.):

```bash
# Enable core dumps globally
ulimit -c unlimited

# Configure core dump location
echo "/tmp/core.%e.%p" | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern

# After crash, analyze:
gdb ./myprog /tmp/core.myprog.12345

# In GDB:
(gdb) bt full          # Full stack trace with all locals
(gdb) frame 3          # Go to the crash frame
(gdb) info locals      # See variables at crash point
(gdb) info registers   # See register state
(gdb) x/8x $rsp        # Examine stack memory
```

## Common Pitfalls

1. **Debug symbols not loaded.** If `bt` shows `??` or `0x0000... in ?? ()`, the binary is stripped or compiled without `-g`. Recompile with `-g`.

2. **Optimizations defeat debugging.** `-O2` can inline functions, reorder code, and eliminate variables. Always use `-O0` for debugging sessions. If the bug only reproduces with optimizations, try `-Og` (debug-friendly optimizations).

3. **Valgrind is slow.** Programs run 10-30x slower under Valgrind. For long-running programs, use ASan instead (only ~2x slowdown). Use Valgrind on targeted test cases, not full production runs.

4. **STL containers are unreadable without pretty-printers.** Install `libstdc++6-*-dbg` matching your GCC version. Test with `(gdb) p my_vector` — if it shows raw internals, pretty-printers are missing.

5. **ASan + Valgrind don't mix.** Don't compile with `-fsanitize=address` and then run under Valgrind — they conflict. Use one or the other.

6. **ASan requires shared ASan runtime.** If you get `error while loading shared libraries: libasan.so`, install: `apt-get install libasan8` (or matching version).

7. **Core dumps with `systemd/coredumpctl`.** Many modern Linux distros use systemd's coredumpctl. Find dumps: `coredumpctl list`, inspect: `coredumpctl gdb <pid>`.

8. **Valgrind + shared libraries.** If Valgrind reports errors in system libraries, use `--suppressions` to filter them out and focus on your code.

9. **Signal handling.** GDB catches signals by default and pauses. If your program uses signals intentionally, use `handle SIGUSR1 nostop noprint` to let them pass through.

10. **Templates.** Function template breakpoints work: `b MyClass<int>::myMethod`. For ambiguous overloads, use the full signature: `b 'MyClass<int>::myMethod(char const*&)'` (quotes important).

## Verification Checklist

- [ ] `gdb --version` prints version info
- [ ] `valgrind --version` prints version info
- [ ] Compile test with `-g`: `g++ -g -o /tmp/test_gdb -xc++ - <<< 'int main() { return 0; }'`
- [ ] GDB can read symbols: `gdb -batch -ex 'info functions' /tmp/test_gdb` shows `main`
- [ ] Core dumps enabled: `ulimit -c` shows `unlimited`
- [ ] ASan works: `g++ -g -fsanitize=address -o /tmp/test_asan -xc++ - <<< 'int main() { int *x = new int; delete x; *x = 5; return 0; }' && /tmp/test_asan` produces ASan error report

## One-Shot Recipes

**"My program crashes with SIGSEGV — where?"**

```bash
ulimit -c unlimited
./myprog              # let it crash
gdb ./myprog /tmp/core.myprog.*
(gdb) bt full         # full backtrace — crash site immediately visible
```

**"Is there a memory leak?"** (quick check)
```bash
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./myprog 2>&1 | grep -E '(definitely|indirectly|possibly) lost'
```

**"Why is this variable wrong at line 42?"** (step through)
```bash
gdb --args ./myprog
(gdb) b myfile.cpp:40
(gdb) r
(gdb) n              # step to line 41
(gdb) p suspicious_var
(gdb) n              # step to line 42
(gdb) p suspicious_var  # see how it changed
```

**"Valgrind says invalid read — where's the actual code?"**
```bash
# Valgrind shows stack traces — look for the first frame in YOUR code, not libc:
# ==12345==    at 0x...: operator delete(void*) (in ...libstdc++...)
# ==12345==    by 0x...: MyClass::~MyClass() (myfile.cpp:23)    <-- THIS ONE
# ==12345==    by 0x...: main (main.cpp:15)
```
